query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A simulation-based predictive approach that explicitly incorporates lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations in high-entropy alloys will yield significantly more accurate predictions of low phonon thermal conductivity compared to current empirical or conventional ab initio methods.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibiting a random multi-element solid solution with substantial atomic-level lattice distortions and chemical fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Implement and calibrate a simulation framework (e.g., combining machine-learned force fields with ab initio molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport theory) that accounts for both lattice distortions and force-constant (and chemical bond) fluctuations.
generation.conditions: Measurements taken over a temperature range (e.g., 300–700 K) where phonon scattering due to lattice distortions is pronounced; applicability is limited to multi-element HEAs (typically 5 or more elements) with significant structural disorder.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice distortion and force-constant fluctuations (on the order of 20–50% variability) that reduce phonon velocities and enhance scattering.
generation.mechanism: The simulation explicitly models how lattice distortion and chemical variability slow phonon propagation and increase scattering events, thereby lowering the lattice thermal conductivity. This detailed treatment should bridge gaps in current predictions that do not fully capture disorder effects found in HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulation predictions will align more closely with experimental measurements of lattice thermal conductivity, reducing the prediction error margin by at least 30% relative to conventional empirical or DFT-only approaches when applied to HEAs with similar disorder.
generation.baseline: Existing prediction approaches that employ empirical rules or traditional ab initio calculations, which typically do not incorporate detailed disorder-induced scattering effects.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective mainly for disordered, multi-element HEAs in the studied temperature range; its accuracy may diminish for materials with lower degrees of lattice distortion, simpler binary/ternary systems, or systems where long-range order dominates.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement may vary depending on the alloy composition and the calibration of simulation parameters (e.g., supercell size effects). There is also uncertainty in how well the methodology scales to HEAs with different elemental combinations or under conditions outside the calibrated temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of HEAs with well-characterized compositions (preferably similar to FeCoCrMnNi or other 5-element systems) and predict their lattice thermal conductivity over a temperature range of 300–700 K using the new simulation-based predictive approach. Independently, measure the phonon thermal conductivity of the same alloys using techniques such as laser flash analysis and inelastic neutron scattering. Compare the simulation predictions with the experimental data.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (κL) at multiple temperatures
Phonon dispersion and attenuation through inelastic scattering techniques
Validation of lattice distortion/force-constant fluctuation magnitudes via complementary structural analyses (e.g., TEM, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation-based predictions deviate by more than 20% from the experimental measurements across the tested temperature range (and this deviation is not attributable to calibration uncertainties or experimental error), then the hypothesis that the new predictive approach significantly improves the accuracy over conventional methods would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The difference in electronegativity (another intrinsic characteristic of element) affects the local chemical bonding and plays a vital role for the properties of high-entropy materials, such as the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys (, , ) for engineered applications, the charge redistribution of high-entropy catalysts () for hydrogen evolution reaction, and the electron transport of high-entropy oxides () for lithium-ion battery. Similar to the mass and strain field fluctuations, the electronegativity difference could increase the complexity of chemical bonding between atoms as the chemical bond fluctuation. Therefore, the contribution of electronegativity difference was also included into the Callaway-Debye model for lattice thermal conductivity calculation (Supplementary Text and table S6). We have found that the chemical bond fluctuation (ΓC) demonstrates a noticeable contribution to lattice thermal conductivity in GeTe-AgSbMn compared to other two samples (Fig. 5B), which is derived from the decreased electronegativity difference of Mn (1.55), Pb (2.33), and Sn (1.96) to other constituent elements Ge (2.01), Ag (1.93), Sb (2.05), and Te (2.10).

Unfortunately they did not calculate the same polarization for the transverse mode along the [ζζ0] direction as we have measured, limiting a direct comparison. The behavior looks similar in these materials and our HEA, with different regimes in longitudinal broadening and a smoother behavior in transverse broadening. One should note however that the low-q part of the spectrum could not be reliably reproduced by the simulation, due to the rather small supercell used. Interestingly, the force-constant fluctuations per atomic pair found from the simulation is between 20 and 50%, in nice agreement with our simplistic estimation for FeCoCrMnNi. This similarity between our 5-elements random alloy and binary and ternary alloys highlights a fundamental contradiction between our data and Mu’s theory, from which, going from 2 to 5 atoms, one would expect a larger phonon attenuation due to the larger variability of the random environments of the atomic pairs. In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.5. Lattice Thermal Conductivity of PbSnTeSe
cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.

chosen.approach: Simulation-based prediction of lattice thermal conductivity in HEAs
